With optimal management, people with type 2 diabetes can live a normal life, but are at risk of multiple complications (/topics/diabetes-type-2/background- information/complications/) long term. Insulin deficiency in type 2 diabetes progresses with time and usually worsens over a period of years [NICE, 2020a (/topics/diabetes-type-2/references/)].

Insulin deficiency in type 2 diabetes progresses with time and usually worsens over a period of years [NICE, 2020a (/topics/diabetes-type-2/references/)]. The International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) guidelines note that type 2 diabetes diagnosed in young people is characterized by rapid onset and progression, with more common and progressive co-morbidities (such as fatty liver disease and sleep apnoea), and more rapid development of microvascular complications and cardiovascular risk than adult-onset type 2 diabetes, leading to increased morbidity and mortality rates [Zeitler, 2018 (/topics/diabetes-type- 2/references/)]. The World Health Organization notes that young-onset type 2 diabetes is associated with greater mortality rates, more complications, and increased cardiovascular disease risk factors than for people with type 1 diabetes of similar duration [WHO, 2019 (/topics/diabetes-type-2/references/)]. © NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) 2025.
